thread.title: Darth Bane's Rule of Two: Canon vs. Legends
thread.hook: One master, one apprentice: where the rule came from, and which parts are still canon.

title: One Master, One Apprentice
logline: Trace Darth Bane’s Rule of Two from its Legends origins to the parts that survive in current Star Wars canon.

plan.title: The Sith Become Two
plan.focus: Open on the stark promise of the Rule of Two, then trace how Darth Bane establishes it in Legends after the Sith’s destruction. Keep the focus on what the Legends account actually says about the rule and Bane’s purpose.

plan.title: What Canon Keeps
plan.focus: Set the Legends account beside current canon: identify what canon states about the Rule of Two and Darth Bane, and what details remain exclusive to Legends. End by distinguishing confirmed lore from tempting assumptions about how much of Bane’s story carried over.

chapter1.title: The Sith Become Two
chapter1.narration:
“One master. One apprentice.” That is the stark promise at the heart of the Rule of Two: a Sith order reduced to a pair, one to embody power, the other to crave it. [c1] In the Legends account, this is not a slogan floating free of history. It is a rejection of a failed system, forged after a war that nearly broke both sides. [c2]

The story begins in the long shadow of the New Sith Wars. After nearly a thousand years of conflict, Jedi and Sith alike stood near collapse. [c3] The eleventh century BBY would later be called the Republic Dark Age, though the record offers little sign of a coherent Sith threat through much of that period. [c4] That distinction matters: a long war does not mean one united enemy marched through every year of it.

Then, in the last decade of the Republic Dark Age, a new Sith power rose. [c5] Jedi Master Skere Kaan turned Dark Lord and founded the Brotherhood of Darkness, also called the Dark Army. [c6] The Brotherhood gathered fragmented New Sith, slaughtered many of its strongest lords, and aimed at the shattered Galactic Republic. [c7]

But Kaan’s answer to division was not a small, disciplined order. It was a brotherhood that claimed equality among Sith Lords and forbade the title “Darth.” [c8] The Rule of Two would replace that model as the guiding principle of the Sith Lords who followed the New Sith Wars. [c9] The contrast is almost theatrical: Kaan says, in effect, “we are equals”; Bane’s system makes succession the whole engine of the order.

And here is the name behind the change. Darth Bane was born Dessel in 1026 BBY, a poor miner on the Outer Rim world of Apatros. [c10] The Legends account credits him with creating the Rule of Two. [c11] It also gives him a cold, practical purpose: the Brotherhood’s leadership looked frail to him, and he wanted the Brotherhood destroyed. [c12]

Bane did not merely wait for the old order to collapse. He contacted the Sith fleet in orbit and ordered it to attack Jedi reinforcements, knowing that the Jedi could then send dropships past the blockade. [c13] His choice turned the Brotherhood’s own military strength into the instrument of its ruin. It is a brutal reversal: the fleet meant to secure victory helps open the way to destruction.

After the Ruusan campaign, Bane still needed someone to inherit the future he was building. [c14] He encountered a young Force-sensitive girl named Zannah, who had been brought to Ruusan by the Jedi months earlier and separated from them. [c15] She had spent her time there trying to survive. [c16] In this account, the apprentice is not an ornament beside the master. She is the next contest, the next threat, and the reason the system must keep moving.

Here is my read: Kaan’s Brotherhood treats unity as a gathering of equals, while Bane’s Rule of Two makes conflict between generations the mechanism of survival. [c17] One Sith order spreads power across a brotherhood; the other concentrates it in a master and an apprentice. [c18] The parallel is explicit in the structure, even if the story’s drama comes from the people trapped inside it.

So: the old Sith emerge from a long, exhausting war, and Kaan builds a brotherhood that claims equality. Bane destroys that system and leaves a pair to carry the Sith forward. [c19] But if one apprentice is meant to surpass one master, what happens when the apprentice is ready?

Next, choose the path: Zannah’s first test, the Rule’s succession gamble, or the fate of the Sith beyond Ruusan.

Zannah’s first test: the apprentice lear.title: Zannah’s First Test
Zannah’s first test: the apprentice lear.narration:
Ambria. Zannah has a datacard holding all of Hetton’s knowledge, and she brings Hetton and his Umbaran minions to attack her master. [c1] The plan has a sharp edge: she is not simply sending enemies at Darth Bane. She is standing close enough to watch what happens when the old master is caught unawares. [c2]

Eight assassins rush Bane. He kills all eight in rapid succession, then kills Hetton, while Zannah watches. [c3] That is her first hard lesson in succession: a clever plan can arrange the test, but it cannot make the master easy to kill. [c4]

And remember what this test is testing. Bane created the Rule of Two because he believed the Sith Order’s infighting was inevitably self-destructive. [c5] The rule leaves two places: master and apprentice. Its design turns ambition into a succession mechanism, with the apprentice meant to grow powerful enough to take the master’s title. [c6]

That means Zannah’s job is a contradiction with teeth. She must learn from Bane, carry his teachings forward, and become dangerous enough to replace him. [c7] If she stays weak, the line fails. If she becomes strong, the master has every reason to fear her. Here’s my read: the Rule of Two is less a peace treaty than a fuse. [c8]

In this Legends account, Zannah is Bane’s apprentice after the war between the Sith and Jedi Orders, chosen to carry the teachings and the Rule of Two forward. [c9] The story gives her no easy inheritance. Her path runs through observation, preparation, and the possibility that one day she must make the lesson personal. [c10]

There is a second measure of her ambition. Zannah wanted an apprentice of her own before attacking Bane, so that if she won, she could continue the Rule of Two’s legacy without delay. [c11] She is already thinking beyond victory. She wants the next link ready before she breaks the present one.

And Bane is not waiting passively for the future. Without Zannah’s knowledge, he investigates the legend of Darth Andeddu’s holocron, said to hold the secret of eternal life. [c12] The master who built a system around being replaced is now looking for a way to outlast replacement. That is the tension in one image: the apprentice preparing a successor, the master searching for more time.

The payoff belongs to Legends, not current canon: Zannah becomes a Dark Lord of the Sith, and Bane’s apprentice is trained to carry the Rule of Two onward. [c13] Her credibility as successor rests not on a clean triumph in this first test, but on the ambition and preparation the account gives her. She studies the master, survives the danger around him, and plans for what comes after him.

So: Bane’s rule makes succession the engine of Sith survival, and Zannah learns that replacing a master requires more than wanting his place. [c14] The apprentice must become powerful enough to end the master’s reign, while preserving the order that makes the struggle matter. [c15]

Where next? We can follow Bane’s search for eternal life, trace Zannah’s plan to claim the mantle, or examine how the Rule of Two reshapes Sith history.

The succession gamble: when should an ap.title: The Moment to Strike
The succession gamble: when should an ap.narration:
A thousand years before the Clone Wars, the Brotherhood of Darkness falls at Ruusan. [c1] Darth Bane survives, and sees what Sith infighting has cost his order. [c2] His answer is not another council, another crowded room of rivals, or another promise that everyone will share power. It is a pair. One master. One apprentice. [c3]

You chose the succession gamble: when should the apprentice strike? In the Legends account, Bane and Zannah do not answer that question quickly. They leave Onderon, take a vessel from a Neimoidian merchant, and settle on Ambria. [c4] There, they spend ten years building an intelligence network with money from Qordis's account. [c5] Their aim is to learn enough to destroy the Jedi and seize galactic control. [c6]

Ten years. That is the first answer: patience is not idleness. It is work conducted out of sight. The apprentice waits, learns, and prepares. The master waits too, because a succession that arrives before the successor is ready is merely another way to lose.

But a hidden network cannot settle the question forever. In Legends, Bane and Zannah eventually confront one another in the Stone Prison. [c7] Zannah corners him more than once and withstands or evades his Force lightning, yet she cannot kill him. [c8] She is defensive by instinct and training, and struggles when she must become the primary aggressor. [c9]

That is the trap. The apprentice has to be dangerous enough to challenge the master, but the challenge itself exposes every weakness. Zannah can hold ground. She can survive. But survival is not succession. The throne does not pass to the person who nearly wins.

Then the contest changes shape. In the Legends account, Bane and Zannah battle for possession of her body, their wills fighting where their weapons once did. [c10] Bane's essence takes hold, and he sees and hears through Zannah. [c11] The succession gamble has become something more intimate and more horrifying than a duel: the master may try to inherit the apprentice instead.

Now set that story beside current canon. The Rule of Two is an essay authored by Bane after Ruusan, and it becomes the cornerstone of his reformed Sith Order. [c12] It is preserved in hidden Sith Archives and passed from master to apprentice for centuries. [c13] In the Republic's last decades, it reaches Darth Sidious, whose public identity is the politician Palpatine. [c14]

That gives us a sharp contrast. Legends supplies this particular Bane-and-Zannah succession drama, including the mind-battle. Current canon establishes the doctrine's long transmission and its arrival with Sidious, but these cards do not establish the Zannah episode as canon. [c15]

Here's my read: Bane is the architect of the test, while Zannah is the apprentice forced to live inside it. Their parallel is not that they are the same person; it is that the rule turns inheritance into a contest between a system's founder and the next generation. Bane wants the Sith legacy to outlast him. Zannah must prove she can take it without becoming merely its vessel.

Strike too soon, and you may lack the strength to finish the master. Wait too long, and the master may decide your strength belongs to him. The Rule of Two makes patience a weapon, but it also makes patience dangerous. Every year spent preparing is another year the master remains in control.

So: Ruusan's defeat gives Bane the reason to replace Sith infighting with a pair. In Legends, Zannah's long preparation leads to a failed killing attempt and a battle for possession; canon carries the Rule forward to Sidious. [c16] The question is still hanging in the dark: when the master and apprentice are both waiting, who moves first—and what story should we follow next: Bane's rise after Ruusan, Sidious inheriting the rule, or another master-apprentice gamble in Star Wars?

Beyond Ruusan: what becomes of the hidde.title: The Sith After Ruusan
Beyond Ruusan: what becomes of the hidde.narration:
Ruusan is quiet at last, but quiet is not the same as safe. You chose to follow the hidden Sith beyond the battlefield, where survival means becoming a secret passed from one pair of hands to another.

The Legends account begins with a battlefield built to end the Sith. In the seventh battle of Ruusan, Jedi Lord Valenthyne Farfalla crushed the Sith in the pivotal engagement. [c1] The battle was the final major engagement of the New Sith Wars, and the thought bomb made this last clash the one people remembered. [c2] Kaan, the Sith leader, unleashed that bomb, destroying every Force-sensitive caught in its blast radius. [c3] Farfalla had already withdrawn with most of the Army of Light, following Lord Hoth’s final orders. [c4]

Now look at the strange figure standing on the edge of that catastrophe: Darth Bane. He wanted to destroy the Brotherhood of Darkness and remake the Sith. [c5] The order’s infighting and greed helped bring defeat at Ruusan in 1032 BBY, as the Jedi nearly destroyed the weakened Sith. [c6] Bane helped the Jedi gain the upper hand by ordering the Sith fleet to break formation and engage them. [c7]

That is the hinge. Bane does not preserve the old Sith by making them larger. In Legends, he answers weakness with radical compression: master and apprentice, power and hunger, one succession at a time. After Bane’s death, Zannah took Cognus as her apprentice, continuing the Rule of Two. [c8] A civilization-sized war machine has become a family business with murder in the job description. That last phrase is my description, not a record.

And what is the pair doing while the galaxy looks elsewhere? The Rule of Two’s establishment coincided with a plan called the Grand Plan: corrupt the Galactic Republic from within, diminish and disgrace the Jedi, then rise and conquer the galaxy. [c9] That is patient ambition on a scale that makes ordinary coups look like impatience with paperwork.

In Legends, the succession carries forward for nearly a thousand years. [c10] Then, in 181 BBY, a fallen Padawan named Kibh Jeen revealed the Sith’s survival and the Rule of Two to the Jedi with his dying words. [c11] Remember the shape of that reveal: not an army returning over the horizon, but one dying voice giving away the existence of a hidden line.

Here’s the contrast you came for. The fuller account of Bane’s survival and the succession described here is Legends material; these cards do not establish that same sequence as current canon. [c12] The Rule of Two is the thread, but the thread runs through different continuities, not one combined biography.

Even the Legends line is not a perfectly obedient chain. The practice continued for a thousand years with varying levels of enforcement. [c13] In 67 BBY, Darth Tenebrous was murdered by his apprentice; Darth Plagueis held the doctrine in contempt and intended to live forever alongside his own apprentice, Darth Sidious. [c14] The rule survives, then bends under the very appetite it was designed to discipline. A Sith can inherit the rule and still dream of being the exception.

So: Ruusan ends the age of open Sith war, and Legends gives Bane a hidden succession that reaches toward the era of Plagueis and Sidious. [c15] The account we have traced is a Legends line, not evidence for that same succession in current canon. [c16] Where should the next journey lead: into the Republic’s slow corruption, toward Plagueis and Sidious testing the rule, or to another empire’s secret machinery?
